question: Despite higher prices, French consumers prefer buying locally produced goods to support their producers and prioritise high-quality products. In theory, country of origin labels build trust. In practice, however, fruit from other countries – particularly Belgium and the Netherlands – is sold as if it had been grown in France, as is the case with Conference pears.

These countries are trying to offload inventory from surplus production that has been created by using plant protection products that are banned in France and by harvesting fruit before it is mature, which changes the flavour but allows the fruit to last longer.

At almost half the price, these pears are often labelled as being of ‘French origin’, hoodwinking consumers, creating large profit margins for the fraudsters and driving down prices. Having conducted 2 500 inspections in France this year, the French Directorate General for Consumer Affairs, Competition and Fraud Control has been overwhelmed by the scale of the phenomenon. In light of the above: 1.
Can the Commission confirm that the ‘administrative assistance and cooperation obligations of Member States’1 are in effect in this particular case?
How does the Commission explain these failings in its role as coordinator of ‘the action undertaken by Member States where instances of non-compliance are widespread or recurrent’2?
Supporter3

As provided for in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2015/1918 pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Ibid. This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Mathilde Androuët (PfE).
answer: 1. As regards checks related to marketing rules, the provisions on administrative assistance and cooperation laid down in Articles 102 to 108 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (the Official Controls Regulation) (1) apply insofar as possible fraudulent or deceptive practices are identified in respect of the marketing standards referred to in Articles 73 to 91 of Regulation (EU) 1308/2013 (2).

National authorities in France have not reported any issues relating to the origin mislabelling of fruits and vegetables within the EU Alert and Cooperation Network (ACN) (3) in 2025. 2. The responsibility for carrying out checks to verify that fruit and vegetables are in conformity with the relevant marketing standards, including origin labelling, lies with the Member States’ inspection bodies.
In case of non-compliance because of defects or deterioration, Member States must notify forthwith the Member States likely to be concerned by the consignment that is not in conformity (4).

Where conformity checks identify possible fraudulent or deceptive practices in respect of the marketing standards, competent authorities should take appropriate action in accordance with the Official Controls Regulation and exchange fraud notifications in accordance with Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715 (5).
